q: Which language can a CPU execute directly, without any translation?
explain: A CPU directly executes machine-code instructions made of 0s and 1s. Assembly and high-level programs must be translated first.

q: Which of the following correctly lists the three basic functional groups of a CPU?
explain: The standard trio is Control Unit, Arithmetic Logic Unit and registers. A 'program unit' is not a CPU component, and RAM is separate main memory.

q: Which CPU unit decodes instructions and coordinates data flow among the processor, memory and I/O interfaces?
explain: The Control Unit interprets instructions, generates control signals and coordinates operations. The ALU only calculates and compares.

q: Which part of the CPU performs comparisons such as equal to, greater than or smaller than?
explain: Comparisons belong to the logic function of the ALU; the control unit then uses the result to direct execution.

q: What are the two broad functional sections of the ALU?
explain: The ALU is divided into arithmetic (addition, subtraction and so on) and logic (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, comparisons).

q: Which statement about the ALU is correct?
options: It executes every instruction on its own
It always calculates square roots directly
Square roots and exponentials may be handled by an FPU, other circuitry or software
explain: ALU capabilities vary. Square roots and exponential functions may use a floating-point unit, specialised circuitry or software, and not every instruction is executed solely by the ALU.

q: Which of the following is NOT a stage of the instruction cycle?
explain: The cycle is fetch, decode, execute (with write back when needed). Installing a device is not a stage, even though software installation uses CPU instructions.

q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
explain: The PC holds the next instruction's address. The IR holds the instruction currently being processed.

q: Which register holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed?
explain: The Instruction Register (IR) keeps the current instruction. PC points to the next one, MAR holds a memory address and MDR holds transferred data.

q: Which register identifies the main-memory location being read from or written to?
explain: MAR holds the main-memory address of the access. MDR (also called MBR) holds the data that moves to or from that location.

q: A register is more specifically classified as which type of circuit?
explain: Registers retain state (commonly using flip-flops), which makes them sequential circuits. 'Digital' is correct but broader.

q: Which statement about the accumulator is correct?
options: It is a separate memory category apart from registers
It is a kind of secondary storage
It is a register that holds operands or results in accumulator-based processors
It is the bus that carries addresses
explain: The accumulator is itself a register. Other processor designs use general-purpose registers to hold results.

q: Which technique helps devices with different data-transfer speeds exchange data smoothly?
explain: A buffer temporarily holds data during a transfer to accommodate differences in the rates at which devices produce and consume data.

q: What does DMA stand for in computer hardware?
explain: DMA means Direct Memory Access: hardware moves data between an I/O device and main memory without the CPU handling every item.

q: What is the main benefit of DMA?
options: It reduces the CPU workload during data movement
It increases the processor clock speed
explain: DMA frees the CPU for other work during transfers. It does not raise clock speed, add RAM or store data permanently.

q: A typical DMA transfer takes place between which two components?
options: An I/O device and main memory
explain: DMA moves data between an I/O device and main memory with limited CPU involvement.

q: Which statement about CPU involvement in DMA is correct?
options: The CPU is completely absent from the process
No setup of any kind is needed
DMA increases the size of RAM
The CPU sets up the transfer, and completion or errors are often reported by an interrupt
explain: CPU involvement is limited, not zero: the CPU and driver configure the transfer, DMA hardware moves the data and an interrupt often signals completion.

q: If registers and cache both appear among the options, which is the fastest?
explain: Registers sit inside the CPU and are the fastest storage level, ahead of cache, RAM and secondary storage.

q: Which is the correct order of storage from fastest to slowest?
explain: The speed hierarchy runs Registers, then Cache (L1, L2, L3), then RAM, then secondary storage.

q: Why is cache memory used in a computer?
explain: Cache keeps copies of data and instructions likely to be reused soon, so the CPU waits less for slower main memory. It supplements RAM and does not replace it.

q: When a request misses in all relevant cache levels, where is the data obtained from?
explain: A miss in one cache level moves on to the next (L1, L2, L3); if all miss, the data comes from main memory, usually RAM.

q: Among registers, L3 cache and RAM, which normally has the greatest capacity?
explain: RAM is generally the largest of these working-memory levels. Registers are the smallest, and secondary storage (not in this comparison) is usually larger still.

q: What is the basic unit used to express clock cycles per second?
explain: Clock frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz is one cycle per second. MHz and GHz are multiples of it.

q: How many cycles per second does a 1 GHz clock produce?
explain: 1 GHz = 1,000 MHz = one billion cycles per second. One trillion would be 1 THz.

q: What does MIPS measure?
options: Instruction throughput: million instructions per second
explain: MIPS counts millions of instructions completed per second. Clock frequency is measured in Hz, not MIPS.

q: How is the length of the clock period related to clock frequency?
options: A longer period gives a higher frequency
A shorter period gives a higher frequency
explain: Frequency = 1 / clock period, so the shorter the period, the higher the frequency.

q: Which statement about CPU speed is correct?
options: A higher GHz alone does not prove that one processor is faster than another
Clock speed means the number of instructions executed per second
Every instruction always takes exactly one clock cycle
Every personal computer runs at 100 KIPS
explain: Performance also depends on IPC, architecture, cores, cache and workload. Cycles are not instructions, and there is no universal 100 KIPS PC speed.

q: Which of the following is directly related to CPU operation?
explain: Clock speed describes the processor's cycles per second. Monitor size, mouse DPI and printer speed relate to other devices.

q: Which pairing of instruction-set design and example is correct?
explain: x86 is the standard CISC example, while Arm and RISC-V are RISC designs.

q: Which statement about cores and multitasking is correct?
options: Multitasking always means truly simultaneous execution
Several cores can execute separate instruction streams at the same time
A uniprocessor system always has several CPUs
explain: Multicore processors run separate instruction streams in parallel. A single core can still multitask by rapid switching (time-sharing).

q: The Intel 4004, the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor, was introduced in which year and with what word size?
explain: The Intel 4004 appeared in 1971 and was a 4-bit processor.

q: The Intel 8086 has a 20-bit physical address bus. How much memory can it address?
explain: 2^20 bytes = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MiB. The 8086 has a 16-bit word and data bus.

q: Which company develops the Ryzen family of processors?
explain: Ryzen (3, 5, 7 and 9) comes from AMD, Advanced Micro Devices, a major competitor of Intel.

q: Which of the following product-company pairs is correct?
explain: Dimensity belongs to MediaTek. Exynos is Samsung's, Snapdragon is Qualcomm's and Grace is NVIDIA's.

q: Which group of companies collaborated on the PowerPC (the AIM alliance)?
explain: AIM stands for Apple, IBM and Motorola. IBM was not the sole developer of PowerPC.

q: Which company announced the Arm-based Grace data-centre CPU in April 2021?
explain: Grace is NVIDIA's Arm-based CPU for demanding data-centre workloads; NVIDIA is otherwise best known for GPUs.

q: What did the abbreviation ARM originally stand for?
explain: Arm began at Acorn as Acorn RISC Machine and was later expanded to Advanced RISC Machines. It was not designed only for phones.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three basic system buses?
explain: The standard three are address, data and control buses. A cache interconnect may exist in a design, but 'cache bus' is not a standard category.

q: Which bus carries read, write and timing signals?
explain: The control bus carries read, write and timing signals; the address bus identifies locations and the data bus carries data and instructions.

q: What does an SMPS (Switched-Mode Power Supply) do in a desktop computer?
options: Converts regulated DC into mains AC
Converts mains AC into regulated DC for the components
explain: The SMPS turns mains AC into regulated DC. It is a system component, not circuitry inside the CPU chip.
